summary: Jonathan Fernandes presents a RAG stack refined through 37 failed attempts, targeting both newcomers and experienced practitioners. The stack components include orchestration (LlamaIndex or LangGraph for prototyping; LlamaIndex for production), embedding models (closed APIs like OpenAI's text-embedding-ada-002 or open models from Nvidia and BAAI's BGE small), vector database (Qdrant for scalability from a few to hundreds of thousands of documents), language models (closed APIs like GPT-3.5 or GPT-4, or open models from Meta and Alibaba's Qwen), monitoring and tracing (LangSmith or Arize Phoenix for prototyping; Arize Phoenix Docker for production), re-ranking (Cohere for closed prototyping; Nvidia for open production), and evaluation (Ragas framework). Prototyping is done in Google Colab for free hardware acceleration; production uses Docker Compose to support on-premise deployment, especially for financial institutions requiring data to stay on-premise. The demo uses a London railway company's HTML knowledge base of 32 documents. A naive RAG solution in LlamaIndex produces an unsatisfactory response about London black cabs. Fernandes explains cross-encoders (high accuracy, poor scalability) and bi-encoders (fast, scalable, less precise), positioning bi-encoders at vector database retrieval and cross-encoders at post-retrieval re-ranking. He systematically swaps components: replacing the in-memory vector database with Qdrant, swapping the default OpenAI embedding for BAAI's BGE small open model downloaded to Colab, and upgrading the LLM from GPT-3.5 turbo to GPT-4 with temperature 0. The improved response about arriving 75 minutes early remains suboptimal. He inspects LlamaIndex source nodes to identify contributing HTML files, then adds a Cohere cross-encoder reranker as a node postprocessor, which produces the best response directing users to booth number five at London St. Pancras International. He emphasizes monitoring with Arize Phoenix or LangSmith to measure component latency, and Ragas for systematic evaluation across many queries. The production environment uses Docker Compose with containerized images for data ingestion, Qdrant, a front-end app, Ollama or HuggingFace TGI for model serving, Phoenix for tracing, and Ragas for evaluation.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The final RAG stack emerged from 37 failed attempts, with learnings organized by pipeline component.
Systematically swapping components—Qdrant for vector DB, BAAI BGE small for open embeddings, GPT-4 for LLM—improves but does not fully solve retrieval quality.
Adding a cross-encoder/reranker (Cohere) as a node postprocessor after vector database retrieval produces the best response.
Bi-encoders belong at the vector database retrieval stage; cross-encoders belong at post-retrieval re-ranking.
Production deployment uses Docker Compose with containerized services: Qdrant, Ollama or HuggingFace TGI, Arize Phoenix, and Ragas.
Prototyping uses Google Colab; production uses Docker for on-premise deployment common in financial institutions.
Monitoring and tracing tools (Arize Phoenix / LangSmith) measure how long each component takes and troubleshoot bottlenecks.
Ragas enables systematic evaluation across many queries rather than testing one question at a time.
LlamaIndex source nodes reveal which files contributed to a response, aiding debugging.
Open models (BAAI, Nvidia) are preferred in production for on-premise requirements, while closed APIs (OpenAI, Cohere) are used for prototyping.

sections.title: Introduction and RAG Stack Overview
sections.summary: Jonathan Fernandes introduces himself and his goal of delivering the most ROI RAG guide per minute. He presents the RAG stack components from 37 failed attempts: orchestration (LlamaIndex/LangGraph), embedding models (closed APIs or open from Nvidia/BAAI), vector database (Qdrant), language models (closed APIs or open from Meta/Qwen), monitoring (Langfuse Phoenix/Arize Phoenix), re-ranking (Cohere/Nvidia), and evaluation (Ragas). Prototyping is in Google Colab; production uses Docker for on-premise needs.

sections.title: Knowledge Base and Naive RAG Demo
sections.summary: He introduces a London train operator knowledge base of HTML files and the query 'Where can I get help in London?' He explains RAG as retrieval, augmented, and generation steps. Using LlamaIndex SimpleDirectoryReader, he loads 32 documents with metadata. A naive RAG solution built in a couple of lines retrieves documents and queries the vector database, but the response about London black cabs is unsatisfactory.

sections.title: Query Processing and Cross-encoder vs Bi-encoder
sections.summary: He discusses adding query processing (removing PII) and post-retrieval steps. He explains cross-encoders, which send query and document through a BERT model producing a 0-1 similarity score, offering accuracy but poor scalability. He then explains bi-encoders, which use two separate BERT-based models for query and document, compare via cosine similarity, and are fast and scalable. He positions bi-encoders at the vector database retrieval stage and cross-encoders at post-retrieval for additional accuracy.

sections.title: Component Swapping, Re-ranking, and Production Setup
sections.summary: He swaps RAG components in code: replacing in-memory vector database with Qdrant, default OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 with BAAI's BGE small open model downloaded to Colab, and GPT-3.5 turbo with GPT-4 at temperature 0. The improved response about arriving 75 minutes early remains suboptimal. He inspects LlamaIndex source nodes to identify contributing HTML files, then adds a Cohere cross-encoder reranker as a node postprocessor, producing the best response directing users to booth number five at London St. Pancras International. He emphasizes monitoring with Arize Phoenix or LangSmith for component latency tracking, and Ragas for systematic multi-query evaluation. He concludes with the production environment: Docker Compose with containerized images for data ingestion, Qdrant, front-end app, Ollama or HuggingFace TGI for model serving, Phoenix for tracing, and Ragas for evaluation.

limitations: Cross-encoders are slow and not scalable as document size grows
Naive RAG solution produces unsatisfactory responses for nuanced queries
Even with component swaps (Qdrant, BGE, GPT-4), response remains suboptimal without reranking
Production on-premise requirements can limit cloud deployment options for financial institutions
